analysis.one_liner: Tightens federal limits on ethylene oxide, a cancer-causing industrial gas, and requires public notice of violations.
analysis.headline: Introduced in November 2018, the bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Ethylene oxide is a gas used to sterilize medical equipment, and the EPA's own scientists concluded it is more carcinogenic than earlier thought. This bill would have required the EPA to rewrite its emission limits for the gas within 180 days, using the agency's December 2016 cancer-risk assessment, apply the strictest available control technology to chamber exhaust vents, and alert the public within 30 days when a facility violated the new limits. If the EPA failed to alert the public, its Inspector General would have to investigate why and what health risks the failure created.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near facilities that emit ethylene oxide — including communities in Illinois such as those around sterilization plants in the Chicago suburbs — would get stricter emission limits and a legal right to timely public notice when violations occur.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the EPA to revise ethylene oxide emission standards based on the agency's own 2016 evaluation of the gas's cancer risk, replacing limits based on outdated science.
It requires the EPA to apply maximum achievable control technology requirements to chamber exhaust vents, the strictest emission-control standard available under the Clean Air Act.

Facilities' violations would have to be made public within 30 days, and a failure to do so triggers an Inspector General investigation into the reasons, the health risks, and how to prevent repeat failures.

analysis.who_pays: Commercial sterilization companies and other industrial facilities that emit ethylene oxide would bear the cost of installing tighter pollution controls and facing public scrutiny of violations; some of that cost could pass through to hospitals and medical-device supply chains.

drawbacks.text: Ethylene oxide is essential to sterilizing much of the nation's medical equipment supply, and the strongest good-faith objection is that sharply stricter rules could raise compliance costs and disrupt the supply of sterilized medical devices if facilities cut back or close.

The bill mandates a timeline of 180 days and prescribes the exact scientific basis for the standards, bypassing the usual notice-and-comment rulemaking process — a shortcut that could invite legal challenges and produce rules that do not survive in court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefit — reducing exposure to a gas the EPA's own assessment identified as a serious cancer risk, plus guaranteed public notice of violations — is substantial for the communities most affected. The costs fall on a small number of industrial emitters, though the mandated 180-day timeline and legislatively fixed scientific basis make the rules legally fragile, and disruption to the medical-sterilization supply chain is a real if manageable risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Durbin, joined by Sen. Tammy Duckworth, introduced the bill on November 28, 2018.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the same day.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was ever recorded, and the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Facilities that emit ethylene oxide avoided the stricter standards and the mandatory public-violation notices, while nearby residents remained unprotected by federal law.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democratic senators sponsored the bill, no Republican support is recorded, and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan breakdown exists.

industries.note: These facilities emit ethylene oxide, the gas the bill targets, and would have had to install stricter pollution controls and face mandatory public notice of violations. Their emissions are the cancer risk the bill addresses, so their interest runs directly against the residents who live nearby.

These companies rely heavily on ethylene oxide to sterilize roughly half of the nation's medical devices; stricter emission rules could raise sterilization costs or shrink capacity, but they also depend on public confidence that sterilized products are made safely.
